sourceInformation.genre: Surgical action with visual-novel medical drama
sourceInformation.perspective: First-person surgeon's-eye close-up on a 3D operating field; talking-head close-ups and 3/4 room shots in story scenes
sourceInformation.tech: Pixel Engine 0.46.0 (riftlight kit: three.js r186, Rapier, WebGPU), own systems in JavaScript, esbuild 0.28.2, AI Hub session client 1.4.0
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's native low-poly 3D rendered as pixel art; procedural painted tissue canvases, original busts, tools, strains and sets; Kenney furniture recoloured for generic props
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's native rig clips on custom figures, SpringChain, LegStepper and Squash, plus procedural bust, tool, heartbeat and breathing animation
sourceInformation.audio: Everything synthesised in code: engine Song chiptune music (10% default), SoundDef effects, Animalese-style gibberish voices from pure-JS formant syllables
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, shared-world, 1 to 4 seats; couch co-op on its own with no network
sourceInformation.testing: Headless tools allowed, unlimited: Node sim, content and real-stage replay tests, the kit check.mjs, Playwright Chromium browser tests with stub pads, a bot playthrough of the whole game, five hub harness runs, screenshots at 1080p. No person played it
sourceInformation.research: The plan's planner read the source's Wikipedia page, the hub's protocol and the engine kit, and ran engine spikes; during the build I read the kit's guides and the hub README, and did no further research on the source

testingFeedback: About 29 in the game: 8 from scripts (balance report, sim tests, the sound lint, which found a misnamed wave making nine sounds and the choirs fail, the kit replay check, which found level swaps racing a replay, and a pad test failing under load, which led to one press acting twice or not at all when the frame rate dipped), about 13 from screenshots, including a Dies Irae crown that never drew. Reading the code against the plan line by line then found 8 more that no test had caught, such as sliders that did not reach a running op and a missing wheel for co-op seats. Two more failures were bugs in the tests themselves.
1, now fixed: Op 4 could not be finished, because two bone fragments hid under pools that were already gone. The balance report found it, and the bot now clears Op 4 at every skill above idle.
The whole game played by the bot in the real page on manual time: every scene, op and screen with the view running, in about a minute.
The rumble check: a stub pad only proves the call path runs, and no script can say how it feels. No person played this game, so feel and real-player difficulty are untested.
engineFeedback: Models as plain data plus the pixel pipeline. A 3D bust from a few boxes and slabs looks like a shipped game, with no art files.

Rarely. wasPressed misses taps when a test presses and releases inside one slow software frame, so tests had to hold keys across frames. check.mjs --headless replays only the last level and never yields, so my async level swaps failed it until I deferred them. Palette-only model colours forced a material swap for skin tones.
The painted tissue canvas: a per-frame 480x270 texture on a displaced mesh, which carries pools, wounds, stitches, gel and guides. Next, per-pad input with analog triggers.
Slow software WebGPU made browser tests timing-sensitive. Manual stepping with engine.step solved most of it.
Per-pad gamepad state with analog triggers built into Input, instead of one merged pad, so couch co-op needs no polling of its own.
promptFeedback: The plan marks what was verified and gives working numbers, so I could trust them and spend the effort on the game.
Very little. The title riff asks for the source name while the plan keeps every other use of it out, so I chose a title that riffs on the second opinion without repeating the name.
Judging hands-on feel and difficulty with no person playing: the bot proves each op can be cleared, not that it feels right.
Say how long a first-time human should take per op, so a bot-based balance report can be checked against something.

aiHub.name: Second Stitch
aiHub.description: A melodramatic surgical action game in pixel art: ten operations against a clock, a terrifying nurse in your ear and a man-made disease called Mercy. Scrub in alone, or with up to four pairs of hands.
aiHub.controls: Stick or mouse moves the tool, R2 or left click uses it, right stick or 1-8 picks a tool, L2 or Space for your gift
